item.description: Up to 911.5 million shares came free at once, more than 140 percent of the public float, while the S&P printed another record high on the largest option-call volume ever recorded.
item.content:encoded:
Up to 911.5 million shares came free at once, more than 140 percent of the public float, while the S&P printed another record high on the largest option-call volume ever recorded.

Yesterday AMD beat and fell ten percent. Today AppLovin grew revenue 53 percent at an 84 percent margin and fell twenty. Two sessions, one verdict: beating stopped being the bar.

Market context. The index does not know any of that. Per the Kalshi list, the S&P printed a new all-time high at 7,730 today, its twenty-fifth record of the year, and Kalshi puts 8,000 before year end at 70 percent. Tom Lee wants 7,900 to 8,000 this month, UBS 8,100 by December.

How it got there is the part to hold onto. Per the Financial Markets list, the Kobeissi Letter counted a record 4.0 million S&P call contracts on Tuesday, against a 700,000 daily average in 2020 and 2021. The put-to-call skew posted its largest two-day decline since 2017. Mr Derivatives supplied the necessary commentary: "Wowzers! What can possssssibly go wrong here?!"

Leadership underneath is thin. $GOOGL fell about 3.5 percent on the DeepMind reshuffle, and per Stocks with Josh the level that matters is $SPY 686, which has held all week. A loss of it opens 629.

The scoreboard.

  • Miss, cleanly. On Tuesday I went 55/45 that SpaceX trades higher today than it closed that night. It is down double digits into the unlock. I said I was trading the mechanics, and the mechanics are what beat me.
  • Resolved on the date. The August 6 lockup I have been flagging since July 16 arrived as advertised: 911.5 million shares, more than 140 percent of the public float.
  • Resolved, and the quarter was not the problem. AppLovin reported August 5 as the scorecard I said it would be. Revenue grew 53 percent and the stock lost a fifth.
  • Standing. My 60/40 that AMD trades above yesterday's after-hours level in a month. It sits at $472, with Jose Najarro raising his target to $750 on $25 of EPS at 30 times forward, and Burry short the complex.

1. SpaceX's float went from 5 percent to 20 percent in one morning. Per the Financial Markets list, over $100 billion of $SPCX shares unlocked today. Per the People to follow list, here is the rest of the queue.

$SPCX unlock scheduleShare of supply
August 6, from a 5 percent IPO floatabout 7 percent, taking tradable to 20 percent
August 21 through December 9about 29 percent more, reaching 40 percent
June 2027Musk eligible, about 46 percent

The print underneath was good and nobody cared. Per Ticker Symbol YOU, revenue was $7.81 billion, up 92 percent, against a $6.93 billion estimate, with EPS of $0.09 against an expected 26-cent loss. Then capex landed just under $18.5 billion, 39 percent above expectations, or $2.35 spent per dollar of revenue, with no 2027 guidance at all.

The stock closed at its lowest price in history yesterday, having shed roughly $1.6 trillion of market value since June's high, per Barchart on the Financial Markets list. Morgan Stanley still carries a $300 target.

The honest comparable is Meta in 2012, down about 50 percent at the 91-day lockup and still down 36 percent a year later. Own it as a compute business with a supply problem that runs four more months.

2. AppLovin grew 53 percent, printed an 84 percent margin, and lost a fifth of its value. Per Daniel Koss on the Stocks list, the quarter was $1.92 billion of revenue, up 53 percent, with $1.61 billion of adjusted EBITDA at an 84 percent margin, and the stock fell 19 percent before the bell.

What broke is smaller and more specific. Per VanquishTrader on the People to follow list, free cash flow conversion fell to 54 percent, buybacks were nearly halved, and management anchored long-term growth closer to 30 percent rather than the 50s. UBS blames a delayed ad-model upgrade and a slow nonendemic ramp, and kept a Buy.

The sell side did not.

$APP price targetFromTo
Piper Sandler, to Neutral$665$385
Scotiabank$775$515
Jefferies, RBC and BTIG$640 to $700$550 to $575

At 24 times forward earnings on a 0.5 PEG, this is a company repriced for decelerating rather than for missing, and the SEC overhang came off in the same quarter. I am 60/40 that $APP is higher in three months.

3. Memory got taken apart at 4am and bought back at the open. Per the Stocks list, $MU fell 29 percent in July, its worst month since June 2005, after a 189 percent year, and sits under $900 with Korea down another 5 percent overnight. Jefferies cut $SNDK from $3,000 to $1,750, a 42 percent haircut, with Citi to $2,100 and Mizuho to $1,900. RBC went the other way, up to $1,300.

Then the tape reversed it. Per ripster47 on the Financial Markets list, $SNDK, $WDC and $MU were all bought at the open.

The reason to fade the panic is contractual. Per Milk Road AI, Bernstein models roughly 35 percent of all memory bits shipped between 2027 and 2029 as locked into take-or-pay contracts (the buyer pays whether or not it takes delivery) at a floor of $0.26 per gigabyte against a $0.29 spot. Micron has taken $22 billion of customer prepayments for chips it has not made across 16 agreements, and its last quarter was $41.6 billion at an 81.2 percent operating margin.

Spot can crack. A take-or-pay floor on a third of three years of supply cannot crack the same way, and I am holding 60/40 that multiples expand before they compress. Dylan Patel, on the Hermes list, explains the premium better than any model: Micron trades above SK Hynix because "corporate governance exists."

4. Eli Lilly put up $23 billion and is losing the pill race it invented. Per Milk Road, $LLY reported $23 billion of revenue against $20.7 billion expected, up 48 percent year over year, with Mounjaro and the GLP-1 franchise at $9.9 billion in the quarter. Jefferies took its target to $1,440, Morgan Stanley to $1,419 and Leerink to $1,309.

The oral is where the fight is. Novo Nordisk sold roughly $495 million of its pill in the quarter against Lilly's $90 million, a five-to-one drubbing in the format that decides the next decade of this market. Lilly's answer is that prescriptions doubled in the last week of July.

That is one week of scripts against a quarter of sales, and I am taking it anyway at 60/40. Injectables were a manufacturing race and Lilly won it. Pills are a distribution race, and a company printing $23 billion a quarter can buy distribution.

5. Burry is short with entry prices, and Eisman will not follow him. Per the Financial Markets list, Michael Burry published his book with the levels attached: short $NVDA at $198, $MU at $1,051, $AMAT at $729, $TSLA at $416, $SOXX at $642 and $PLTR at $161, verdict "WE ARE NEAR A MAJOR TOP AND POSSIBLY A 1987-TYPE FALL." Per NoLimitGains on the Stocks list, the S&P is up more than 100 percent since he last told people to sell, in January 2023.

Steve Eisman's refusal is the more useful position. Per Prof G Markets, Eisman says "he doesn't have a data point that you and I don't have," and names his trigger precisely: "I need a price war in the LLM world." Until inference pricing collapses, the capex holds.

What sits against him is the customer base. Bloomberg puts 70 percent of Microsoft's AI revenue on OpenAI, Barclays 75 percent of Amazon's on OpenAI and Anthropic, UBS 30 percent of Google Cloud on the same pair. OpenAI lost $21 billion last year, Anthropic roughly $11 billion. Meta meanwhile grew revenue 28 percent against 55 percent expense growth and produced $785 million of free cash flow.

I am 60/40 with Eisman, and the 40 is that concentration number. A price war is not the only way this breaks. One of two customers slowing its orders does it.

Single names worth your watchlist.

  • $SPCX. Float tripled today and reaches 40 percent by December 9. The business beat by a billion and guided to $100 billion of run-rate revenue exiting 2026. Every buyer until Christmas fights a published supply schedule, so let the calendar work.
  • $APP. A 53 percent grower at 24 times forward with an 84 percent EBITDA margin, sold off because management stopped promising the 50s. Free cash flow conversion at 54 percent decides whether the deceleration is mix or model.
  • $LLY. $23 billion and 48 percent growth, and the next move is about a pill it sells at a fifth of Novo's rate. Three targets went up this week. September script data settles it.
  • $SNDK. Jefferies cut it 42 percent and RBC raised it inside the same 24 hours, and it bought back its premarket lows. Still the cleanest live read on whether NAND pricing is rolling over.
  • $CCJ. Bank of America raised its 2027 uranium forecast to $130 a pound, roughly 52 percent above spot, on utility contract coverage falling to 48 percent from 56. Target trimmed to $133, Buy kept. Oklo reaching first criticality at its Groves Test Reactor the same week is the demand side showing up.

item.title: AMD beat and fell ten percent, and that is the whole market in one print
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: Bank of America's 7,741 target for the year is done, the S&P closed an entire candle outside its upper Bollinger band for the first time since March 2024, and SpaceX guided to a $100 billion run rate.
item.content:encoded:
Bank of America's 7,741 target for the year is done, the S&P closed an entire candle outside its upper Bollinger band for the first time since March 2024, and SpaceX guided to a $100 billion run rate.

Yesterday I said SpaceX reported into a 34 percent short interest and nobody had a model. It beat and guided to a $100 billion exit run rate. AMD is the more instructive print, because it beat too and got sold ten percent.

Market context. The Hormuz route agreement Macro covers tonight took the last of the war premium out and the tape went vertical. The Nasdaq rose more than 3 percent.

Per Walter Bloomberg on the Market list, Bank of America says the S&P has reached its 2026 target of 7,741, with technicals pointing to 8,000, then 8,234 and potentially 8,541. It sees 7,500 as key support and warns weak August-to-October seasonality, stretched momentum and Friday's payrolls could cap it.

Heisenberg has the stretched part measured. For the first time since March 2024, the entire S&P candlestick body closed outside the upper Bollinger band, by a wide margin. Sunday it was Tesla outside the lower band. Four sessions later the index is outside the upper one.

The scoreboard.

  • Resolved, and it beat. SpaceX reported $7.8 billion of June-quarter revenue against a $6.8 billion expectation and guided to a $100 billion exiting run rate. Per Gene Munster, that implies a December quarter near $22 billion, and December revenue estimates went up about 17 percent.
  • For, after being against. I marked Shay Boloor's Lag-7-becomes-Mag-7 call against on Monday when equal-weight led. A 3 percent Nasdaq day is the other side of that, and the call is live again.
  • Standing. My 60/40 that the July low holds into mid-August runs to August 15 and is not in doubt at a record high.
  • Due tonight. SanDisk reports with an implied move of roughly 15 percent either way.

1. AMD beat, and the market decided that was not enough. Per Con on the Stocks list, AMD produced good numbers and fell about 10 percent after hours having closed the regular session up 7 percent near its highs. It had nearly tripled over the prior year and was up 140 percent year to date going in.

Two things did it. The beat was modest against expectations that were not, and capex rose while free cash flow fell. For a name priced on operating leverage that is the wrong shape regardless of the earnings line.

The read-through is the point. Con concludes AI names now have to beat by a lot rather than merely beat, and he is selling his AI enabler positions on it, naming resistance at $NBIS $220 to $230 and $MU $900, with $AAOI, $NET, $MTSI and $ASYS reporting within days and Nvidia, Marvell and Micron behind them.

The other side is specific and worth holding. Per Shay Boloor on the Market list, Futurum reiterated a Buy with an $800 target, raising its 2027 forecast to $90 billion of revenue and $17.50 of EPS, including $29 billion from server CPUs and $39 billion from data centre GPUs on the Venice ramp, Helios shipments to Meta, Oracle and OpenAI, and up to 14 gigawatts of committed accelerator deployments. That last figure is contracted rather than modelled.

My lean is 60/40 that AMD trades above today's after-hours level in a month. A sell-the-news reaction to a beat in a name up 140 percent is positioning rather than thesis.

2. SpaceX guided to $100 billion and left a $350 billion funding gap. The print was good. The arithmetic behind the guidance is the story.

Per Gene Munster, guidance implies about $8.5 billion of monthly revenue in December, and the Street sits near $100 billion for 2027, up 122 percent. Munster thinks that is low, and at 5 percent month-over-month growth off December he gets $135 billion. His caveat is the honest one: the cloud contracts carry 90-day cancellation provisions, and he waves it away because inference is in the top of the first.

Per SouthernValue on the Stocks list, here is the part nobody guided.

SpaceX capacity and fundingFigure
Data centre capacity todayabout 1.4 GW
End of 2026 target2 GW
2027 targetclose to 10 GW, all Nvidia
Implied capex at $50-60bn per GWroughly $500 billion
Cash on handabout $100 billion
Cash from operations, first half 2026$3 billion
Anthropic and Google spot GPU dealsabout $26 billion of annual recurring revenue
Estimated exit-2026 forward operating cashabout $50 billion
Residual funding gapabout $350 billion

His conclusion is the one to carry: Nvidia customer financing has to come into play. Which puts SpaceX in the same structure as the OpenAI campus, with the chip supplier underwriting the buyer.

3. CXMT refused to cut prices for Apple, and that breaks the bear case on memory. Per Jukan on the Market list, South Korean media reports Apple negotiated with CXMT over mobile DRAM supply prices including LPDDR5X, to ease cost pressure on its next iPhone lineup, and CXMT rejected the request. It insisted on prices higher than or comparable to Samsung and SK Hynix.

If that holds it inverts the story I cut my memory call on. Monday's headline was CXMT doubling capacity past 600,000 wafers a month, and the market read new Chinese supply as a price war. A supposed price-breaker declining to undercut the incumbents on a marquee account is the opposite behaviour, and it says CXMT is optimising for margin rather than share.

The honest caveat is that The AI Investor, relaying the same report, called it "fake news to me, doesn't pass the smell test." He may be right and the sourcing is one media report.

So I am raising the memory call back to 60/40 that multiples expand before they compress, from 55/45 Monday, and doing it on a single-sourced report I have flagged as contested. SanDisk reports tonight into a 15 percent implied move and settles it faster than any of this.

4. The humanoid race got a supply chain this week. Per Wayne Liang on the Market list, four separate national efforts moved at once.

  • Mitsubishi is converting an idle engine plant to build roughly 1,000 humanoids a month
  • Unitree lists in China in a couple of weeks, holding 85 percent of 2025 shipments with more than $20 billion of subsidies behind it
  • Hyundai is targeting a few thousand a year through Boston Dynamics
  • Tesla is ramping Optimus

The tradeable part: downstream flow benefits $CCXI and Agility as the only US-listed pure-play, and he flags plainly that a SPAC merger is higher risk and higher reward.

Converting an engine plant is the detail. The constraint has moved from whether humanoids work to who has idle precision-manufacturing capacity. That is an industrials question, and Japan has more of it than anyone.

5. Gold outran everything and the leadership underneath is not what the index says. Gold rose more than 4 percent to above $4,300, with the tracking fund running from roughly $370 to almost $392 in two sessions. That is a record equity tape and a gold breakout in the same week.

Per AskLivermore on the Stocks list, the dispersion underneath is severe.

Year to dateMove
$SPY+2.59 percent
$QQQ-1.93 percent
$XLK-2.34 percent
$SMH-11.03 percent

Semis down 11 percent while the broad index is up is not a tech-led market, whatever a 3 percent Nasdaq day suggests. His own book is up 5.49 percent, he is staying cautious short term precisely because everyone turned bullish, and his next buys are homebuilders, education providers, micro and small-business enablers, and aging-population REITs. He recently sold Mastercard for a 13 percent gain and added Arm and Marvell.

Single names worth your watchlist.

  • $AMD. Beat and fell 10 percent after hours on capex up and free cash flow down. Futurum's $800 target rests on 14 gigawatts of committed accelerator deployments, contracted rather than hoped for. This is a positioning reset in a name that had tripled, not a thesis break.
  • $SNDK. Reports tonight with a roughly 15 percent implied move, and it has reacted positively to four of its first five prints since listing. This is the cleanest read on whether commodity DRAM pricing is actually cracking after the CXMT headlines.
  • $SPCX. Beat at $7.8 billion and guided to a $100 billion exit run rate, with the first big lockup opening tomorrow. The funding gap is roughly $350 billion and the answer is probably Nvidia's balance sheet, so own it as a compute business rather than a launch business.
  • $CCXI. The only US-listed pure-play on humanoid components into Mitsubishi at a thousand units a month, Unitree's listing and Optimus ramping. A SPAC structure means size it like the option it is.
  • $GLD. Up four percent above $4,300 while equities printed records and oil fell. If gold is a monetary signal it is the most important chart on the board. If McGlone is right that it is a sock puppet to the S&P, it is beta with better marketing.
  • $XHB. Homebuilders are on AskLivermore's buy list and the cleanest expression of a rate path where six desks disagree. They win on Citi's cut scenario and lose on Kashkari's.

item.title: SpaceX reports tonight with 34 percent of its float sold short
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: Ninety-five percent of borrowable SpaceX stock is already out on loan, the first $100 billion lockup opens Thursday, and Caterpillar just cleared $20 billion of quarterly sales for the first time.
item.content:encoded:
Ninety-five percent of borrowable SpaceX stock is already out on loan, the first $100 billion lockup opens Thursday, and Caterpillar just cleared $20 billion of quarterly sales for the first time.

Yesterday SpaceX printed an all-time low the session before its first earnings report. Today it bounced into the print, and the borrow data says almost everyone has already picked a side.

Market context. The oil move Macro covers this evening did the work here. Futures hit a record high on Bessent's Hormuz comments, and the index arrives at the level that has capped it since spring.

Per Scott Redler on the Financial Markets list, the S&P cleared the 7448 line and pushed to 7610 in the prior session, and the index "may be trying to leave its 10-plus week range." He wants it to hold above 7448, with 7620 the bigger level overhead. Frank Cappelleri's 7,680 target from late April is still live per Ryan Detrick, and Societe Generale now carries 8,000 on broadening earnings strength.

Leadership is the part that does not fit the record. The equal-weight S&P keeps outrunning the cap-weighted index and the rotation is carrying into August. That is not what a megacap-led tape looks like. Tonight's SpaceX and AMD prints land in tomorrow's edition.

The scoreboard.

  • Against, on day one. I carried Shay Boloor's call yesterday that the Lag 7 turn back into the Mag 7 and the generals lead again. The equal-weight index outrunning the cap-weighted one is the opposite of that, and the rotation is where the money actually went.
  • Standing, and improving. My 60/40 that the July low holds into mid-August is intact with futures at a record. The call runs to August 15.
  • Due tonight. AMD reports, and SpaceX reports for the first time in company history.
  • Due Thursday. The first SpaceX lockup, more than $100 billion of stock, begins unlocking two days after the print.

1. The SpaceX print is the most crowded short in the market. Per zerohedge on the Financial Markets list, S3 data shows 95 percent of SpaceX stock available to borrow is out on loan, and short interest is 34 percent of the float. The stock hit an all-time low near $104 yesterday and traded back to $118 before the open.

Per Kyle Reidhead on the Crypto list, here is what the print actually turns on.

LineWhere it stands
Expected revenue$6.8 billion
Expected cash burn$10.9 billion
Starlink ARPU$99 in 2023, $66 last quarter, street wants $65.50
AI capex last quarter$7.7 billion, 76 percent of all company spending
Anthropic compute deal$1.25 billion a month through 2029
2026 X revenue, consensusabout $2.9 billion
Consensus EPSa $1.26 loss to a $0.33 profit

That last row is the tell. When the sell side's range spans a loss and a profit, nobody has a model, and a 34 percent short interest into a no-model print is a squeeze setup rather than a thesis.

Heisenberg's framing is the honest one and it is worth quoting: it is so obvious the stock goes down tomorrow that it becomes obvious not to short it, because everyone thinks it is obvious. My lean is 55/45 that SpaceX trades higher on Thursday than it closes tonight, and the reason is mechanical rather than fundamental. The lockup is the real event, and a squeeze into a supply cliff is how the worst entries get made.

2. Caterpillar cleared $20 billion in a quarter for the first time, and the reason is data centres. Per the Financial Markets list, Caterpillar surged as quarterly sales topped $20 billion for the first time in company history, driven by the AI data centre build. Heisenberg's read was two words and a question mark: the AI boom is just getting started.

This is the cleanest version of a trade that keeps being mispriced. Everyone argues about whether the hyperscalers earn a return on $860 billion of capex. Caterpillar does not need them to. It sells the generators, the earthmoving and the power equipment into the build, books the revenue on delivery, and carries none of the residual-value risk that makes the neocloud arithmetic fail.

The same logic ran through Vertiv, which raised full-year guidance across the board and still fell double digits, and it is why the picks-and-shovels layer keeps being the least crowded way to own the theme.

3. Memory is being repriced on supply for the second session running. Yesterday Reuters had CXMT weighing a second Beijing fab that would take its capacity past 600,000 wafers a month, and I cut my memory call to 55/45 on it. Today the complex is still working out what that means.

Per the Financial Markets list, Marvell is soaring, and Scott Redler had Nvidia, Micron, SpaceX and SanDisk as the four names on his premarket board. The distinction that matters has not changed since Kyle Reidhead drew it: CXMT's new capacity is commodity DRAM, and high-bandwidth memory is sold out through 2026.

So the right way to hold this is that a China supply headline hits the commodity end and the margin structure, while the AI-critical end stays contracted. I am staying 55/45 that memory multiples expand before they compress, unchanged, because nothing today touched the HBM book. SanDisk reports tomorrow and is the better read on where commodity pricing actually is.

4. The Hormuz war trades are unwinding before the war ends. There is a whole trade built on the closure, and it has spent two sessions going the wrong way. The names are Frontline in tankers, RTX in defence and ExxonMobil in energy, and each one was priced off a strait that stays shut and shipping that stays rerouted.

Bessent's draft-text comment takes the top off all three at once. Brent at $81.50 after a 4.7 percent Monday fall is not a war premium, it is the market pricing a signature.

The asymmetry now runs the other way. If a deal lands this week these names give back the rest of the move, and if Iran denies it for a fourth time they gap back. Anas Alhajji's open question decides the medium term: can Saudi Arabia actually reroute 6 million barrels a day through the northern Red Sea? Nobody has answered it, and until somebody does the tanker trade has a floor under it that the defence names do not.

5. Apple is down five straight and starting to trade like a defensive. Per Heisenberg on the Financial Markets list, Apple is holding $300 after five down days and a peak-to-trough fall of more than 13 percent, and it has been inversely tracking the Nasdaq proxy.

His setup is the interesting part rather than the level. Once the Nasdaq takes a breather after a large five-day run, he expects defensive money to rotate back into Apple for a bounce. That is a rotation argument dressed as a chart, and it fits the breadth data better than the megacap-leadership story does.

The overhang is real and it is not priced out. Apple guided September below consensus and blamed the memory shortage explicitly, and Bloomberg has MacBook Air orders slipping to September on the same crunch. A component squeeze that delays the best-supplied hardware company in the world does not clear because the stock got cheap.

Single names worth your watchlist.

  • $SPCX. Reports tonight into 34 percent short interest with 95 percent of the borrow already lent, then more than $100 billion of stock starts unlocking Thursday. The print and the supply cliff are 48 hours apart, so anything you do here is a position on the sequencing rather than on the business.
  • $CAT. First $20 billion quarter in company history on data centre demand, and it carries no residual-value risk on the GPUs. The cleanest non-AI way to own the AI build, and the one nobody argues about at dinner.
  • $AAPL. Holding $300 after five down days and 13 percent off the high, inversely tracking the Nasdaq. A defensive bounce candidate with a real memory-cost overhang into September, so size it as a trade and not a thesis.
  • $FRO. The tanker leg of the Hormuz trade, and the one with a floor under it, because rerouting 6 million barrels a day through the Red Sea is unsolved even if the strait reopens. Rates stay elevated on distance travelled rather than on risk.
  • $SNDK. Reports tomorrow and is the honest read on commodity DRAM pricing after the CXMT capacity headline. High-bandwidth memory is sold out through 2026, so this print tells you about the other end of the market and not about the AI book.
  • $VRT. Raised full-year guidance across the board and fell double digits anyway. Either the market knows something about power-equipment margins or that is the kind of reaction that reverses.
